listing_view.reasoning: Subscription reached ~89x by the close day [verified figures], which indicates strong demand into a modest ₹1,529 mn issue priced at ~13.7x latest basic EPS against a stated benchmark of 18.3x — a discount setup auction buyers clearly treated as attractive. However, 0.44x on day one and a 44x jump on the final morning reads like classic last-day NII/financing-driven piling-in, the least reliable kind of signal. There is no GMP or anchor data, so conviction beyond the subscription tape is thin.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue compounding ~29% over two years, a ₹12,047 mn order book (2.7x latest revenue) quoted as of June 2026 [business, page 245], and a stated order-book-backed growth narrative [business, page 248] support the top line. But the quality of earnings is poor: operating cash flow was negative ₹121 mn in the latest year, so reported profit did not arrive as cash [verified figures], and ROCE has slid from 47.5% to 28.8% as the company scales. Improvement in receivable days to 19.5 is genuinely encouraging, but I cannot see what the money converted into instead.

governance.reasoning: There is a live show-cause notice from the Department of Commercial Taxes [litigation, page 445], promoter personal guarantees and unsecured loans to the company [promoters, page 325, page 358], and our figures show a balance-sheet inconsistency where the document's debt-to-equity of 0.23 does not reconcile with its own underlying numbers (computed 1.184). None of this is disqualifying, and the company declares no SEBI actions [litigation, page 445], but a printed leverage ratio that doesn't tie out, in the seller's own document, deserves a discount, not a pass.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Latest-year operating cash flow is negative ₹121 mn against PAT of ₹433 mn, so the income statement is running ahead of the cash reality.
The document prints debt-to-equity of 0.23 while its own components imply ~1.18 with debt rising to ₹2,294 mn; if the balance sheet itself is unreliable, every downstream ratio is suspect.
The company itself flags that future business procurement may become more uncertain, and the entire growth case rests on the ₹12,047 mn book converting on time and on budget.
Inability to recover additional expenses or manage time overruns could hit financials — the exact failure mode when a fixed-price contractor scales quickly.
A September 2023 notice from the Department of Commercial Taxes is disclosed on the face of the RHP and is unresolved at filing.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Not receivables: receivable days collapsed from 94 to 19.5 over the two years, so collections actually got much faster while operating cash flow turned negative ₹121 mn. That means the cash is sitting somewhere else — almost certainly inventory/contract work-in-progress given rising revenue and the company's own overrun risk language — but the extracts I was given contain no inventory or working-capital schedule, so I cannot prove it. What I can rule out from the numbers is that slow-paying customers are the culprit.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A cash-flow statement showing the negative OCF is one-off timing (e.g., a large year-end unbilled-revenue build that unwinds) rather than structural working-capital hunger, plus resolution of why the printed debt-to-equity diverges from the balance sheet. Anchor investor quality and the fresh-issue/OFS split would also move the listing view materially.
